     1	# Rung C3 — Activated abilities: giving the player something to *do* with the board
     2	
     3	> Revision 1 (2026-08-27). This rung replaced a planned deck-knowledge rung after that one's Codex
     4	> plan-review found four blockers for two clauses; the reasoning is recorded at the top of
     5	> `2026-08-27-rung-c6-deck-knowledge.md`.
     6	
     7	## Context
     8	
     9	Ten of the starter deck's 28 printed clauses work. Every one of them is **triggered** — something happens to
    10	a card and the ability fires. The player never chooses to use an ability, because there is no way to: the
    11	`Command` union has `castCharacter`, `castSummon`, `declareAttack`, `declareBlock` and the answer commands,
    12	and **nothing for activating an ability** (`packages/engine/src/commands.ts:5`).
    13	
    14	That single gap blocks **eight** of the eighteen remaining clauses:
    15	
    16	| Card | Clause | Cost | Source zone |
    17	|---|---|---|---|
    18	| Red Mage (1-121C) | Choose 1 Forward, it gains Haste | `[Lightning]` + `[Dull]` | field |
    19	| Noel (16-092C) | Dull all Forwards opponent controls | `[Dull]` + put into Break Zone | field |
    20	| Miner (20-074C) | Draw 1 | `[2]` + `[Dull]` + put into Break Zone | field |
    21	| Undead Princess (19-052C) | Choose 1 Forward, +4000 | put into Break Zone | field |
    22	| Undead Princess (19-052C) | Choose 1 Earth Forward, +2000 | remove from game | **Break Zone** |
    23	| Geomancer (18-064C) | Draw 1 | `[Earth]` + discard itself | **hand** |
    24	| Red Mage (18-069C) | Draw 1 | `[Lightning]` + discard itself | **hand** |
    25	| Sphene (27-126S) | Return a Forward broken this turn to hand | `[0]`, once per turn | field |
    26	
    27	They also reuse almost everything that already exists: the `Effect` AST for the effect half, and `Payment`
    28	(`commands.ts:4`) — dulled Backups and discards — for the CP half, which is the same machinery casting
    29	already uses.
    30	
    31	**This is the rung a human notices.** Ten triggered clauses make a board that happens to you; activated
    32	abilities are the first thing that makes it a board you *use*.
    33	
    34	## Scope: the first four, all from the field
    35	
    36	Building all eight at once would drag in three new capabilities at once (a hand-sourced ability, a
    37	Break-Zone-sourced ability with a removed-from-game zone, and this-turn/once-per-turn tracking). The rung
    38	stays small by taking only clauses whose source card is **on the field** and whose costs are CP, dulling, and
    39	self-break:
    40	
    41	**In:** Red Mage 1-121C, Noel's second clause, Miner's second clause, Undead Princess's first clause.
    42	**Out (C4):** the two hand-sourced `discard itself` Backups; Undead Princess's second clause and the
    43	removed-from-game zone; Sphene's `[0]` (needs "put into the Break Zone from the field during this turn" and
    44	once-per-turn state).
    45	
    46	Four clauses, one new command, no new zones. It also happens to cover every cost shape in the "in" list
    47	exactly once, which is the point of choosing these four.
    48	
    49	## Decisions
    50	
    51	| # | Decision | Ruling (and why) |
    52	|---|---|---|
    53	| C3-1 | **One new command: `activateAbility { player, card, clause, payment }`** | `clause` indexes into the card's ability list, so a card with two activated abilities is unambiguous. `payment` is the **existing** `Payment`, validated by the **existing** CP machinery — an activated ability's CP cost is not a different kind of cost from a cast's, and giving it its own path would be the beginning of two payment systems. |
    54	| C3-2 | **Costs are a declared list on the ability, paid atomically before any effect runs** | `cost: { cp?: {amount, element?}, dull?: true, selfBreak?: true }`. All of it is paid, or none of it is and the command is not legal. CR §1.3.3: an ability's cost is paid on activation, and the effect resolves afterwards — so a Noel that dulls and breaks itself has already left the field when "dull all opponent Forwards" resolves, and must still resolve. This is exactly the frame/agenda separation C1 built, so the effect half needs no new machinery. |
    55	| C3-3 | **`[Dull]` requires the card to be active, and is not payable by a card that entered this turn** | CR §9.3.2 — a Character cannot use a `[Dull]` ability the turn it enters unless it has Haste. The engine already tracks `enteredTurn` for attack legality; this reuses it rather than inventing a second notion of summoning sickness. |
    56	| C3-4 | **Self-break as a cost bypasses `cannotBeBroken`** | C2 already recorded this distinction and it is now load-bearing: "put into the Break Zone" as a *cost* is not the *break* action, so Cloud's future "cannot be broken" must not make Noel's ability unusable. The primitive is a plain zone move that produces a `ZoneTransition` (so C2's watchers still see it), distinct from `breakCard`. |
    57	| C3-5 | **MVP0-SIMPLIFICATION: activation is restricted to the turn player during Main Phase 1 or 2** | The real rules let action abilities be used whenever a player has priority. MVP0 has no stack and `priority` is always the turn player (`state.ts:47`), so there is no window in which a non-turn player could act anyway. Restricting to the Main Phases is therefore not a further loss of fidelity — it is the honest statement of what the existing priority model can already express. Marked at the site, and listed in the README's deviations. |
    58	| C3-6 | **`legalCommands` enumerates activations, and the AI gets them for free** | `candidateCommands` and the browser choice set are both built from `legalCommands`, so an activation that is legal is automatically searchable and clickable. The AI needs no special casing — but see the risk below about whether it will *use* them. |
    59	| C3-7 | Not in scope | The four deferred clauses above; EX Burst; static abilities (Class Tenth Moogle's Lightning CP, Odin's cost reduction, Sphene's Break-Zone protection); deck knowledge (rung C6). |
    60	
    61	## What could go wrong, in the order it will bite
    62	
    63	- **The AI will under-use these, and the win-rate gate will not notice.** `evaluate` scores material and
    64	  tempo. Dulling all the opponent's Forwards has no material term at all, and self-breaking a Forward to pump
    65	  another looks like a *loss* of material to a function that counts bodies. Four clauses is far below the
    66	  noise floor of a mirrored run either way, so **the strength gate here is a regression guard, not evidence
    67	  the AI plays them well** — the same statement the last three rungs have had to make, and the reason the
    68	  acceptance criteria below test reachability and correctness directly rather than through win rate.
    69	- **Cost/effect atomicity is the subtle one.** An ability whose cost removes its own source is the normal
    70	  case here, not the exotic one: three of the four break or dull the source. Any implementation that reads the
    71	  source card while resolving the effect will work for Red Mage and break for Noel.
    72	- **A dulled Backup is both a CP source and a cost.** `[Lightning][Dull]` on Red Mage means *pay one Lightning
    73	  CP* (by dulling some other Backup or discarding) *and* dull Red Mage itself. Paying the CP by dulling Red
    74	  Mage would be paying the same cost twice; the payment validator must exclude the source.
    75	- **Once the AI can dull its own Backups for abilities, it can strand itself** with no CP for its main phase.
    76	  That is a legitimate strategic mistake, not a bug — worth watching in the fuzzer, not worth guarding.
    77	
    78	## Acceptance criteria
    79	
    80	- **C3-A1** Each of the four clauses is reachable from `legalCommands` alone in a real game, and resolving it
    81	  produces its printed effect. (The B-A2-style sweep: drive seeded games and assert every new command shape
    82	  is offered, rather than constructing the position by hand.)
    83	- **C3-A2 (atomicity)** Noel's ability resolves "dull all the Forwards opponent controls" **in full** even
    84	  though its own cost has already put Noel into the Break Zone; Undead Princess's +4000 applies to a chosen
    85	  Forward after Undead Princess has left the field.
    86	- **C3-A3 (cost validation)** An activation is illegal when: the source is dulled, the source entered this
    87	  turn without Haste, the CP payment is short, the payment dulls the source itself, or it is not the
    88	  activating player's Main Phase. Each is a separate test, and each asserts the command is absent from
    89	  `legalCommands` rather than merely rejected by `apply`.
    90	- **C3-A4 (self-break is not a break)** A source with `cannotBeBroken` can still pay a self-break cost, and
    91	  the resulting zone change is visible to C2's observers (a watcher on "an opponent's Forward is broken" must
    92	  **not** fire, because this is not a break — assert both halves).
    93	- **C3-A5** The browser offers activations as ordinary choices, with the printed cost in the label, and a
    94	  human can use all four in a driven game.
    95	- **C3-A6** `ABILITY_CLAUSES` drops by four; the amber "not implemented" warnings stop naming them; the
    96	  marker audit passes.
    97	- **C3-A7** `pnpm test`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm lint`, `pnpm --filter @fftcg/web build` green; fuzzer 200/200
    98	  zero failures; ISMCTS still beats greedy over a mirrored run (regression guard only — see above).

   101

     1	# Rung C6 (DEFERRED) — Looking at your own deck: the information model
     2	
     3	> **Status: deferred, deliberately, after its own Codex plan-review found four blockers.** Revision 1 was
     4	> written as the next rung; the review is
     5	> `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-c3-deck-knowledge.codex-review.md`. Everything below is revision 1
     6	> as reviewed — kept intact because the analysis is sound and this rung will be built eventually. What changed
     7	> is only *when*.
     8	
     9	## Why this is deferred, and what it would cost
    10	
    11	The review found four blockers, none of them cosmetic, and together they describe a substrate rather than a
    12	feature:
    13	
    14	1. **`FieldView.deck` cannot be the knowledge model.** `PlayerState` has no knowledge state at all, so after
    15	   Reeve bottoms two known cards nothing records that its controller still knows those positions. And
    16	   `(CardId | null)[]` cannot express *"unknown to me, known to them"* — which is precisely what a root
    17	   determinisation must preserve about an opponent who has looked at their own deck. Knowledge has to live
    18	   durably in `GameState` as a per-card `knownBy` mask, projected per viewer.
    19	2. **`determinise` must REBUILD a deck pending, not copy one.** Redacting the opponent's candidates leaves
    20	   nothing executable, and a redacted `Pending` cannot be live state at all — `invariants.ts:62` requires
    21	   `max <= candidates.length` and every candidate to exist. That forces a `PendingState` / `PendingView`
    22	   split and a reconstruction step from the AST plus the sampled deck.
    23	3. **Collapsing the action key would make the search play its opponent at RANDOM.** This one was my error and
    24	   it is worth recording precisely: `search.ts:386` groups commands sharing a key and picks among them
    25	   uniformly, so collapsing all of an opponent's private Reeve choices into one key does not model hidden
    26	   information — it replaces the opponent's decision with a coin flip, the exact defect the existing
    27	   actor-view keying was built to avoid. The fix is two identities (an actor/policy key and an observer
    28	   transition key), not one collapsed `ActionKey`.
    29	4. **The browser log leaks the private choice outright.** AI commands are narrated from the AI's own view
    30	   (`useGame.ts:222`) and `describeChoice` names every chosen target (`commands.ts:241`), so an AI Reeve would
    31	   print the card it took straight to the human. Narration has to be observer-relative.
    32	
    33	## Why something else goes first
    34	
    35	The decisive argument is arithmetic, and the review's own scoping section supports it. This substrate buys
    36	**two** ability clauses (Reeve's and Miner's ETBs). Meanwhile **eight** clauses in the same starter deck are
    37	activated abilities — Red Mage's `[Lightning][Dull]`, Noel's `[Dull], put into the Break Zone`, Miner's
    38	`[2][Dull]`, Undead Princess's two, Geomancer's and Red Mage 18-069C's `discard`, and Sphene's `[0]` — and
    39	every one of them is blocked on a single missing thing: there is no `activateAbility` command in the `Command`
    40	union at all (`packages/engine/src/commands.ts:5`). They reuse the existing `Effect` AST for their effect half
    41	and the existing `Payment` machinery for their CP half.
    42	
    43	Eight clauses behind one primitive beats two clauses behind four blockers, and activated abilities are also
    44	the ones a *human* feels: they are the difference between a board you watch and a board you use. Deck
    45	knowledge is deferred until the cards that need it outnumber the cost of the substrate — Hugh Yurg's search
    46	and EX Burst both push in that direction.
    47	
    48	**When this is picked up again, start from the review, not from this spec.** Its staging advice stands: build
    49	the information substrate first with no cards attached, then Reeve alone to prove private pinning, redaction,
    50	rebinding and non-interference, then Miner to prove public visibility, known-opponent-hand persistence,
    51	observer-relative narration, and the browser rendering the reveal at all — the board currently shows deck
    52	count only (`Board.tsx:57`), so a "public" reveal would today be visible to nobody.
    53

    55	
    56	*Revision 1 follows, unchanged.*
    57	
    58	## Context
    59	
    60	Ten of the starter deck's 28 printed ability clauses work. The next ones in line all touch a zone no ability
    61	has touched yet — the **deck** — and the engine cannot currently express them for a reason that is not about
    62	targeting at all.
    63	
    64	`Pending.chooseTargets` carries materialised `CardId`s (`packages/engine/src/state.ts:36`). `viewFor` copies
    65	`state.pending` wholesale to **both** players (`packages/engine/src/view.ts:33`), and `determinise` mints
    66	fresh ids for every hidden card and then copies the stale pending ids over the top
    67	(`packages/engine/src/determinise.ts:41`). So a deck target today would be simultaneously **orphaned** for the
    68	player choosing (ids that name nothing in their view) and **leaked** to the player not choosing. Neither is a
    69	bug in targeting; both are the absence of a model for *who knows what*.
    70	
    71	## The two cards, and why they are one card
    72	
    73	| | Miner (20-074C) | Reeve (20-105C) |
    74	|---|---|---|
    75	| Trigger | ETB | ETB (printed `EX BURST`) |
    76	| Sees | **reveal** the top 5 — public | **look at** the top 3 — private |
    77	| Takes | 1 **Backup** among them → hand | 1 **card** among them → hand |
    78	| Rest | to the bottom of the deck, in any order | to the bottom of the deck, in any order |
    79	
    80	Structurally identical: *expose N from the top, take one matching a filter, bottom the rest.* They differ only
    81	in **N**, in the **filter**, and in **who is allowed to watch**. That last difference is the whole rung — it is
    82	the smallest pair of cards that forces the private/public distinction to be built properly rather than fudged,
    83	which is exactly why they are the right two to do first.
    84	
    85	As with Noel and Lightning in C1, the printed `EX BURST` tag on Reeve is quoted but not implemented: the
    86	clause fires on a normal cast, which is what `enterField` means. EX Burst itself stays out of scope.
    87	
    88	## Decisions
    89	
    90	| # | Decision | Ruling (and why) |
    91	|---|---|---|
    92	| C3-1 | **Knowledge is per player, and lives in the view's deck** | `FieldView.deckCount: number` becomes `FieldView.deck: readonly (CardId \| null)[]` — one slot per card, non-null **only** where that viewer legitimately knows what is there. The count is `deck.length`, so nothing is lost. This is the minimal representation that can express "I know my top 3 but not my fourth", which is precisely what Reeve creates. |
    93	| C3-2 | **`determinise` pins what is known and samples the rest** | Non-null slots keep their id and code and are removed from the unseen multiset before shuffling, exactly as field and hand cards already are (`determinise.ts:38`). Everything else is sampled as today. Without this, an AI that looked at its own top 3 would re-randomise them the instant it tried to think about them — the search would be reasoning about a deck it had just been told it did not have. |
    94	| C3-3 | **`viewFor` redacts pending candidates the viewer cannot see** | A `chooseTargets` whose candidates include hidden cards is filtered to those visible **to that viewer**, and carries `hidden: number` for the remainder. The opponent of a Reeve therefore sees "choosing 1 of 3 cards" and no identities. Redaction happens at the view boundary, not at the prompt, because the view boundary is the only place that knows who is asking. |
    95	| C3-4 | **A private choice by the OPPONENT must key on what was observed, not on what was sampled** | In ISMCTS, an opponent's private deck choice is re-sampled every determinisation. Keyed by card identity, one real decision would shatter into dozens of tree nodes that the searcher can never tell apart in play — and each would be conditioned on information the searcher does not have. Action keys for a non-root player's private choice collapse to the observable form (`take 1 of N from deck`). This is the D2 review's warning that "Reeve's private look invalidates the search's assumption that every action becomes public", answered. |
    96	| C3-5 | **`reveal` and `look at` are one primitive with a visibility flag** | `lookAt { count, visibility: 'public' \| 'private', filter, take }`. Public grants the knowledge to both players, private only to the controller. Building these as two effects would duplicate the ordering, filtering and bottoming logic to express a difference of one field. |
    97	| C3-6 | **MVP0-SIMPLIFICATION: "in any order" becomes a fixed order** | The rest go to the bottom in their revealed order; the player is not asked to arrange them. Asking would add a permutation decision (4 cards = 24 orderings) to every Miner, for cards going to the **bottom of a 40+ card deck**, which in a game this length will almost never be drawn. Marked `MVP0-SIMPLIFICATION` at the site with this reasoning, and listed in the README's deviations. |

A universal pipeline is over-built for this rung, and the honest cure for that is scope, not ambition.    448	   145	     3	## BLOCKER
   449	   146	     4	
   450	   147	     5	**Staleness is tested at the wrong boundary; `respond()` cannot prove that React drops stale results.**
   451	   148	     6	
   452	   149	     7	`respond(init, request)` is pure and synchronous, so it has no knowledge of the outstanding request or current game state (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d2-search-worker.md:19`). Yet D2-A4 proposes testing staleness by driving `respond` out of order (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d2-search-worker.md:35`). The vulnerable operation is `commit`, which unconditionally replaces `stateRef.current` and appends logs (`apps/web/src/game/useGame.ts:253`). A reply can race:
   453	   150	     8	
   454	   151	     9	- `restart()` replacing `stateRef.current` before React runs effect cleanup (`apps/web/src/game/useGame.ts:274`).
   455	   152	    10	- Any human `choose()` that commits another state (`apps/web/src/game/useGame.ts:262`); notably, concede remains legal even when the human is not acting (`packages/engine/src/legal.ts:19`).
   456	   153	    11	- StrictMode’s effect setup/cleanup/setup cycle (`apps/web/src/main.tsx:8`, `apps/web/src/game/useGame.ts:285`).
   457	   154	    12	- Unmount, after which the callback must not call `commit`.
   458	   155	    13	
   459	   156	    14	**Fix:** The minimum acceptance rule is:
   460	   157	    15	
   461	   158	    16	```ts
   462	   159	    17	mounted &&
   463	   160	    18	activeRequestId === result.requestId &&
   464	   161	    19	stateRef.current === requestedState &&
   465	   162	    20	actingPlayer(requestedState) === AI
   466	   163	    21	```
   467	   164	    22	
   468	   165	    23	Then clear the active request before applying, re-check the command against `legalCommands(requestedState, AI)`, and commit from that same state. Every restart, external commit, effect cleanup, and unmount must synchronously invalidate the active ID; unmount must also terminate the worker. Test the main-thread receiver/controller with deferred replies after restart, human commit, StrictMode cleanup, and unmount. Keep `respond` testing only deterministic translation.
   469	   166	    24	
   470	   167	    25	**Search seeds must be stable per game position, not consumed per effect/request attempt.**
   471	   168	    26	
   472	   169	    27	The protocol carries a seed but never defines its allocation (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d2-search-worker.md:17`). The synchronous agent currently advances its RNG once per actual decision (`packages/ai/src/ismcts/agent.ts:64`). A naïve worker port that advances a ref when the effect posts will consume an extra seed during StrictMode, retries, stale requests, or worker replacement (`apps/web/src/game/useGame.ts:285`). Development and production can therefore choose different moves from the same game.
   473	   170	    28	
   474	   171	    29	**Fix:** Derive the search seed from `(gameSeed, committedAiDecisionIndex)`, or cache one seed against the captured state generation. Increment the decision index only when an AI command successfully commits; retries of the same position must resend the same seed. Do not derive it from `requestId`.

   476	   173	    31	## MAJOR
   477	   174	    32	
   478	   175	    33	**The Vite worker form and raw workspace TypeScript are sound, but production worker bundling is not an acceptance gate.**
   479	   176	    34	
   480	   177	    35	`new Worker(new URL('./worker.ts', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' })` is Vite’s supported static form, and Vite emits it as a separate production chunk. Linked monorepo packages are treated as source when they export ESM, which these do (`packages/ai/package.json:5`, `packages/engine/package.json:5`). `server.fs.allow: ['../..']` correctly covers them in development (`apps/web/vite.config.ts:4`), but that option is dev-only; production uses the separate bundler path. See the [Vite worker documentation](https://vite.dev/guide/features#web-workers), [linked-dependency behavior](https://vite.dev/guide/dep-pre-bundling.html#monorepos-and-linked-dependencies), and [`server.fs.allow`](https://vite.dev/config/server-options.html#server-fs-allow).
   481	   178	    36	
   482	   179	    37	The divergence hazard is therefore not a known incompatibility—it is that D2-A7 runs tests/typecheck/lint but no web build (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d2-search-worker.md:40`). A dev probe cannot catch production chunk generation, hashed asset loading, or deployment MIME/base-path failures.

   559	   256	     9	~254 ms/decision. **The browser still plays `GreedyAgent`** — D1 was headless by design, because 254 ms of

   565	   262	    15	## Architecture: three layers, because the races must be testable
   566	   263	    16	
   567	   264	    17	Revision 1 put worker lifecycle, pacing, retries, fallback and stale-result handling into `useGame`'s AI
   568	   265	    18	`useEffect`. That hook already owns state, pacing, mutation and the agent loop; adding this to it would make
   569	   266	    19	every D2-specific race a matter of React timing folklore rather than a test.
   570	   267	    20	
   571	   268	    21	1. **`protocol.ts`** — discriminated message types and the pure `respond(init, request)`. Deterministic
   572	   269	    22	   translation only; no lifecycle, no knowledge of what is outstanding.
   573	   270	    23	2. **`worker.ts`** — a thin shell: store init, `try`/`catch`, `postMessage`. Vitest cannot drive a real
   574	   271	    24	   `Worker`, so the shell deliberately contains nothing worth testing.
   575	   272	    25	3. **`SearchCoordinator`** — one worker per mounted hook. Owns generation/request tracking, stable
   576	   273	    26	   per-position seeds, the pacing deadline, the watchdog, termination, and the `GreedyAgent` fallback.
   577	   274	    27	   **This is the layer the D2 tests target**, because this is where every race lives.
   578	   275	    28	
   579	   276	    29	`useGame` then does what it already does: capture a state, ask for a command, re-check legality against that
   580	   277	    30	exact state, narrate, commit.

   582	   279	    32	## Decisions
   583	   280	    33	
   584	   281	    34	| # | Decision | Ruling (and why) |
   585	   282	    35	|---|---|---|
   586	   283	    36	| D2-1 | A **discriminated wire contract** | `type: 'init' \| 'search' \| 'result' \| 'error'`. Init carries the two declared deck lists **and the stable search configuration** (`rolloutCommandCap`, `explorationC` — `SearchInput` requires them and revision 1's request listed only seed and iterations). Errors carry their `requestId`, or `null` for an init failure, and post **plain strings, never `Error` objects**. |
   587	   284	    37	| D2-2 | **Decks and config at init; the view per request** | `PlayerView` carries `defs` by design and the UI needs them; the search already clones a state containing the same definitions once per determinisation, so one 18-card catalogue per request is not the dominant cost. Revision 1 called this "measured as negligible" — **it was not measured**; D2-A2 now reports the actual serialized size and posting duration, and `Omit<PlayerView,'defs'>` is revisited only if the catalogue materially grows. |
   588	   285	    38	| D2-3 | **Search seeds are stable per game POSITION** | Derived from `(gameSeed, committedAiDecisionIndex)`, incremented **only when an AI command successfully commits**. Never from `requestId`. A seed advanced when the effect *posts* is consumed again by StrictMode's double-invoke, by a retry, by a stale request and by worker replacement — so dev and prod would choose different moves from the same board, which is the worst kind of "works on my machine". |
   589	   286	    39	| D2-4 | **A result is accepted only under all four conditions** | `mounted && activeRequestId === result.requestId && stateRef.current === requestedState && actingPlayer(requestedState) === AI`. Then clear the active id *before* applying, re-check the command against `legalCommands(requestedState, AI)`, and commit from that same captured state. Restart, any external commit, effect cleanup and unmount must **synchronously** invalidate the active id; unmount must also terminate the worker. Note the non-obvious racer: **concede is legal even when the human is not the acting player**, so a human `choose()` really can commit mid-AI-turn. |
   590	   287	    40	| D2-5 | **Pacing is a deadline, not an added delay** | `notBefore = startedAt + AI_STEP_MS`; when the result arrives, schedule at `Math.max(0, notBefore - performance.now())`. A fast search still waits out the 600 ms; a 750 ms search applies immediately, having already shown 750 ms of thinking. Revision 1's "apply at `max(elapsed, AI_STEP_MS)`" was ambiguous enough to be implemented as an *extra* 600 ms. |
   591	   288	    41	| D2-6 | **Fall back to `GreedyAgent`, detect every way it can fail, and say so** | Greedy, not reduced-iteration main-thread ISMCTS: the latter is still a synchronous search with variable rollout cost, which gives up the one guarantee this rung exists for. Detection must cover **missing `Worker`, constructor failure, synchronous `postMessage` clone failure, `error`, `messageerror`, a typed `WorkerError`, and a worker that is killed or hangs and simply never replies** — the last needs a startup and per-request **watchdog**, because nothing correlated ever arrives. On failure: invalidate the request, terminate the worker, switch to Greedy **permanently for that game**, append **one** visible log warning, and play Greedy against the current state under the same pacing deadline. |
   592	   289	    42	| D2-7 | **The iteration budget is measured in the browser** | D1's 200 was an implementation default, never calibrated. Measure, choose, and record the number with the machine and browser it came from. If the browser budget lands well below 200, **the opponent a human faces is weaker than the one D1 measured**, and that gets said. |
   593	   290	    43	| D2-8 | Not in scope | Any change to the search, its keys or its evaluation; a worker pool or parallel search; C3's ability clauses. |

   596	   293	    46

   598	   295	    48	dev logged `worker sees searchIsmcts as: function`, and `vite build` emitted a **52 kB worker chunk**
   599	   296	    49	separate from the 275 kB app chunk. `new Worker(new URL(…, import.meta.url), { type: 'module' })` is Vite's

   601	   298	    51

   603	   300	    53	"cleared", which was too strong. `server.fs.allow` is dev-only; production takes a different bundler path,
   604	   301	    54	and hashed asset loading, MIME and base-path failures all live there. Hence D2-A7 below.

   606	   303	    56	## Acceptance criteria
   607	   304	    57	
   608	   305	    58	- **D2-A1** The browser plays a **full game to a result** against ISMCTS, end to end, no uncaught errors.
   609	   306	    59	- **D2-A2 (honest non-blocking measurement)** On a **production preview**, over N AI decisions: mark
   610	   307	    60	  request-post, response and commit; observe **`longtask` entries** (any reported entry is ≥ 50 ms by
   611	   308	    61	  definition); record the **maximum `requestAnimationFrame` gap**; inject a harmless test button and record
   612	   309	    62	  **input-to-handler** while a search is active. Report browser, machine, iterations, sample count, max long
   613	   310	    63	  task, max frame gap, max input delay, and worker round-trip p50/p95 — plus the request's serialized size
   614	   311	    64	  and posting duration (D2-2). *"No main-thread task ≥ 50 ms during N AI searches"* is a result;
   615	   312	    65	  *"well under 600 ms"* is not, and was revision 1's wording.
   616	   313	    66	- **D2-A3 (determinism across the boundary)** The same `(view, seed, iterations, caps)` through `respond`
   617	   314	    67	  returns exactly the command a direct `searchIsmcts` call returns.
   618	   315	    68	- **D2-A4 (staleness, at the right layer)** Tested against the **coordinator**, not `respond`: deferred
   619	   316	    69	  replies delivered after a restart, after a human commit (including concede), after StrictMode cleanup, and
   620	   317	    70	  after unmount must all be dropped, and the worker terminated on unmount.
   621	   318	    71	- **D2-A5 (fallback)** Each detectable failure — no `Worker`, constructor throw, clone failure, `error`,
   622	   319	    72	  `messageerror`, typed error, and a never-replying worker — switches to Greedy, logs **one** warning, and
   623	   320	    73	  still finishes a game.
   624	   321	    74	- **D2-A6** The chosen iteration budget is recorded with the measurement that produced it.
   625	   322	    75	- **D2-A7** `pnpm test`, `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm lint` **and `pnpm --filter @fftcg/web build`** green, plus
   626	   323	    76	  a **production-preview** browser run that loads the emitted worker asset, completes a real `postMessage`
   627	   324	    77	  round trip, and asserts ISMCTS is actually playing rather than the fallback. Headless gates untouched
   628	   325	    78	  (462 tests, ISMCTS 90.0 % vs greedy, strict fuzzer 0 failures).

   630	   327	    80	## Risks
   631	   328	    81	
   632	   329	    82	- **Staleness is intermittent by nature**, and it is the reason for the coordinator layer. A late result
   633	   330	    83	  applied to a moved-on board corrupts a game rarely and unreproducibly.
   634	   331	    84	- **The fallback can hide itself.** If the worker silently fails the game keeps working and simply plays
   635	   332	    85	  worse — hence one visible warning, and hence D2-A7 asserting ISMCTS rather than merely "a game happened".
   636	   333	    86	- **Seed drift between dev and prod** (D2-3) would be diagnosed as a search bug and is not one.
   637	   334	    87	- **D1's caveats stand**: the iteration budget was never strength-calibrated, and rollouts are ~117× the
   638	   335	    88	  tree cost.

  2055	  1752	+    state = apply(state, agent.decide(viewFor(state, p), legalCommands(state, p))).state
  2056	  1753	+  }
  2057	  1754	+  throw new Error(`seed ${seed} never reached an AI decision`)

  2129	  1826	 # Rung D2 — The search in a Web Worker: the browser gets the strong opponent
  2130	  1827	 
  2131	  1828	+> Revision 2 (2026-08-27), after a Codex plan-review that found two blockers and corrected two claims of
  2132	  1829	+> mine. The review is `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-d2-search-worker.codex-review.md`.
  2133	  1830	+
  2134	  1831	 ## Context
  2135	  1832	 
  2136	  1833	 D1 is merged (`b22be0f`): headless SO-ISMCTS beats `GreedyAgent` **90.0 %** over 120 mirrored games at
  2137	  1834	 ~254 ms/decision. **The browser still plays `GreedyAgent`** — D1 was headless by design, because 254 ms of
  2138	  1835	-synchronous search would block the main thread and freeze the board mid-turn.
  2139	  1836	+synchronous search would freeze the board mid-turn.
  2140	  1837	+
  2141	  1838	+D2 is the wiring only. The search core does not change: `searchIsmcts(input): SearchResult` is already
  2142	  1839	+pure, synchronous and structured-cloneable, which is what D1 was told to leave behind.
  2143	  1840	+
  2144	  1841	+## Architecture: three layers, because the races must be testable
  2145	  1842	+
  2146	  1843	+Revision 1 put worker lifecycle, pacing, retries, fallback and stale-result handling into `useGame`'s AI
  2147	  1844	+`useEffect`. That hook already owns state, pacing, mutation and the agent loop; adding this to it would make
  2148	  1845	+every D2-specific race a matter of React timing folklore rather than a test.
  2149	  1846	 
  2150	  1847	-D2 is the wiring, and only the wiring. The search core does not change: `searchIsmcts(input): SearchResult`
  2151	  1848	-is already pure, synchronous and structured-cloneable, which is exactly what D1 was told to leave behind so
  2152	  1849	-this rung would not have to rewrite it.
  2153	  1850	+1. **`protocol.ts`** — discriminated message types and the pure `respond(init, request)`. Deterministic
  2154	  1851	+   translation only; no lifecycle, no knowledge of what is outstanding.
  2155	  1852	+2. **`worker.ts`** — a thin shell: store init, `try`/`catch`, `postMessage`. Vitest cannot drive a real
  2156	  1853	+   `Worker`, so the shell deliberately contains nothing worth testing.
  2157	  1854	+3. **`SearchCoordinator`** — one worker per mounted hook. Owns generation/request tracking, stable
  2158	  1855	+   per-position seeds, the pacing deadline, the watchdog, termination, and the `GreedyAgent` fallback.
  2159	  1856	+   **This is the layer the D2 tests target**, because this is where every race lives.
  2160	  1857	+
  2161	  1858	+`useGame` then does what it already does: capture a state, ask for a command, re-check legality against that
  2162	  1859	+exact state, narrate, commit.
  2163	  1860	 
  2164	  1861	 ## Decisions
  2165	  1862	 
  2166	  1863	 | # | Decision | Ruling (and why) |
  2167	  1864	 |---|---|---|
  2168	  1865	-| D2-1 | A **typed worker protocol**, not ad-hoc `postMessage` | `WorkerInit` (the two declared deck lists, sent once), `WorkerSearchRequest` (`requestId`, `view`, `seed`, `iterations`), `WorkerSearchResult` (`requestId`, `command`, `diagnostics`) and `WorkerError`. Every one structured-cloneable. Codex's D1 review flagged that the seam *promised* this and did not have it. |
  2169	  1866	-| D2-2 | **Decks at init; the view per request** | Decks are what the search needs and the view does not carry. `PlayerView` already carries `defs`, so a request re-sends the 18-card catalogue — measured as negligible against a 600 ms turn, so **it is left alone**. Stripping `defs` and rehydrating in the worker is available if measurement ever says otherwise; doing it now would be optimising a cost nobody has shown. |
  2170	  1867	-| D2-3 | **A pure `respond(init, request)` the worker merely wraps** | The same trick that made D1 testable: all protocol logic lives in a plain function, and `worker.ts` is a thin `onmessage` shell. Vitest cannot drive a real `Worker`, so anything inside the shell is untestable — the shell therefore contains nothing worth testing. |
  2171	  1868	-| D2-4 | **Requests are generation-checked; stale results are dropped** | `requestId` increases monotonically; the hook ignores any result that is not the one it is waiting for. Restarting a game, or the human acting while the AI thinks, must not have a late result applied to a board that has moved on.   2178	  1875	+| D2-1 | A **discriminated wire contract** | `type: 'init' \| 'search' \| 'result' \| 'error'`. Errors carry their `requestId`, or `null` for an init failure, and post **plain strings, never `Error` objects**. |
  2179	  1876	+| D2-2 | **Decks and config at init; the view per request** | `PlayerView` carries `defs` by design and the UI needs them; the search already clones a state containing the same definitions once per determinisation, so one 18-card catalogue per request is not the dominant cost.   2180	  1877	+| D2-3 | **Search seeds are stable per game POSITION** | Derived from `(gameSeed, committedAiDecisionIndex)`, incremented **only when an AI command successfully commits**. Never from `requestId`. A seed advanced when the effect *posts* is consumed again by StrictMode's double-invoke, by a retry, by a stale request and by worker replacement — so dev and prod would choose different moves from the same board, which is the worst kind of "works on my machine". |
  2181	  1878	+| D2-4 | **A result is accepted only under all four conditions** | `mounted && activeRequestId === result.requestId && stateRef.current === requestedState && actingPlayer(requestedState) === AI`. Then clear the active id *before* applying, re-check the command against `legalCommands(requestedState, AI)`, and commit from that same captured state. Restart, any external commit, effect cleanup and unmount must **synchronously** invalidate the active id; unmount must also terminate the worker. Note the non-obvious racer: **concede is legal even when the human is not the acting player**, so a human `choose()` really can commit mid-AI-turn. |
  2182	  1879	+| D2-5 | **Pacing is a deadline, not an added delay** | `notBefore = startedAt + AI_STEP_MS`; when the result arrives, schedule at `Math.max(0, notBefore - performance.now())`. A fast search still waits out the 600 ms; a 750 ms search applies immediately, having already shown 750 ms of thinking. Revision 1's "apply at `max(elapsed, AI_STEP_MS)`" was ambiguous enough to be implemented as an *extra* 600 ms. |
  2183	  1880	+| D2-6 | **Fall back to `GreedyAgent`, detect every way it can fail, and say so** | Greedy, not reduced-iteration main-thread ISMCTS: the latter is still a synchronous search with variable rollout cost, which gives up the one guarantee this rung exists for.   2251	  1948	-  supported form; the workspace packages are raw TypeScript, so the worker bundle must resolve them the same

  2409	  2106	     4	
  2410	  2107	     5	**Staleness is tested at the wrong boundary; `respond()` cannot prove that React drops stale results.**
  2411	  2108	     6	
  2412	  2109	     7	`respond(init, request)` is pure and synchronous, so it has no knowledge of the outstanding request or current game state (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d2-search-worker.md:19`). The vulnerable operation is `commit`, which unconditionally replaces `stateRef.current` and appends logs (`apps/web/src/game/useGame.ts:253`). A reply can race:
  2413	  2110	     8	
  2414	  2111	     9	- `restart()` replacing `stateRef.current` before React runs effect cleanup (`apps/web/src/game/useGame.ts:274`).
  2415	  2112	    10	- Any human `choose()` that commits another state (`apps/web/src/game/useGame.ts:262`); notably, concede remains legal even when the human is not acting (`packages/engine/src/legal.ts:19`).
  2416	  2113	    11	- StrictMode’s effect setup/cleanup/setup cycle (`apps/web/src/main.tsx:8`, `apps/web/src/game/useGame.ts:285`).
  2417	  2114	    12	- Unmount, after which the callback must not call `commit`.
  2418	  2115	    13

 11052	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-c3-deck-knowledge.md:42:| C3-1 | **Knowledge is per player, and lives in the view's deck** | `FieldView.deckCount: number` becomes `FieldView.deck: readonly (CardId \| null)[]` — one slot per card, non-null **only** where that viewer legitimately knows what is there. Keyed by card identity, one real decision would shatter into dozens of tree nodes that the searcher can never tell apart in play — and each would be conditioned on information the searcher does not have. Action keys for a non-root player's private choice collapse to the observable form (`take 1 of N from deck`).  11446	    80	  /** Σ of ROOT-perspective rewards backed up through this edge. Actor-awareness lives in selection, not here. */
 11447	    81	  reward: number

 11449	    83	}
 11450	    84	
 11451	    85	export interface SearchNode {
 11452	    86	  /**
 11453	    87	   * Who decides here. A function of the `ObservationKey` that created the node (it carries `priority` and the
 11454	    88	   * whole `pending`), so it cannot legitimately differ between visits — `descend` throws if it ever does,
 11455	    89	   * which is a direct check that the observation key is fine-grained enough to identify a decision point.
 11456	    90	   */

 11458	    92	  visits: number
 11459	    93	  readonly edges: Map<ActionKey, SearchEdge>
 11460	    94	}
 11461	    95	
 11462	    96	/** One selection step, kept so backpropagation knows which siblings were AVAILABLE at each node (D-4). */
 11463	    97	export interface PathStep {
 11464	    98	  readonly node: SearchNode
 11465	    99	  readonly edge: SearchEdge
 11466	   100	  readonly available: readonly ActionKey[]
 11467	   101	}
 11468	   102	
 11469	   103	export function createNode(actor: PlayerId): SearchNode {
 11470	   104	  return { actor, visits: 0, edges: new Map() }
 11471	   105	}
 11472	   106	
 11473	   107	/** The edge for `key`, minted on demand. Availability bookkeeping creates edges for actions never selected. */
 11474	   108	export function edgeFor(node: SearchNode, key: ActionKey): SearchEdge {
 11475	   109	  const hit = node.edges.get(key)
 11476	   110	  if (hit) return hit
 11477	   111	  const made: SearchEdge = { key, visits: 0, availability: 0, reward: 0, children: new Map() }
 11478	   112	  node.edges.set(key, made)
 11479	   113	  return made
 11480	   114	}
 11481	   115	
 11482	   116	export const meanReward = (edge: SearchEdge): number => (edge.visits === 0 ? 0 : edge.reward / edge.visits)
 11483	   117	
 11484	   118	/**
 11485	   119	 * What the ACTOR at this node is trying to maximise (D-5). Rewards are always stored from the root player's
 11486	   120	 * point of view, so an opponent node maximises `1 - mean`: the reflection of the root's reward on [0, 1].
 11487	   121	 * Drop the flip and the search builds a cooperative opponent that walks into its own losses — legal, plausible
 11488	   122	 * play that a win-rate gate cannot distinguish from a working search.
 11489	   123	 */
 11490	   124	export function exploitation(edge: SearchEdge, actorIsRoot: boolean): number {
 11491	   125	  const mean = meanReward(edge)
 11492	   126	  return actorIsRoot ? mean : 1 - mean
 11493	   127	}
 11494	   128	
 11495	   129	/** `UCB(s,a) = mean(s,a) + C * sqrt( log A(s,a) / N(s,a) )` (D-4), with `mean` read through the actor. */
 11496	   130	export function ucb(edge: SearchEdge, actorIsRoot: boolean, c: number): number {
 11497	   131	  if (edge.visits === 0) return Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY   // untried: expanded before anything is compared
 11498	   132	  return exploitation(edge, actorIsRoot) + c * Math.sqrt(Math.log(Math.max(1, edge.availability)) / edge.visits)
 11499	   133	}
 11500	   134	
 11501	   135	export function backpropagate(path: readonly PathStep[], reward: number): void {
 11502	   136	  for (const step of path) {
 11503	   137	    step.node.visits++
 11504	   138	    step.edge.visits++
 11505	   139	    step.edge.reward += reward
 11506	   140	    for (const key of step.available) edgeFor(step.node, key).availability++
 11507	   141	  }
 11508	   142	}

 11510	   144	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 11511	   145	// RNG streams (D-8)
 11512	   146	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 11513	   147	
 11514	   148	/**
 11515	   149	 * Three streams, so a change in how many worlds get sampled cannot silently reshuffle which action gets
 11516	   150	 * expanded, and a tie-break cannot reach back into world sampling. All three are seeded from the one `seed`,
 11517	   151	 * so a decision is still reproducible from `(view, seed)` alone.
 11518	   152	 */
 11519	   153	export interface Streams { world: Rng; expand: Rng; tie: Rng }
 11520	   154	
 11521	   155	export function makeStreams(seed: number): Streams {
 11522	   156	  return { world: seedRng(seed), expand: seedRng((seed ^ 0x9e3779b9) >>> 0), tie: seedRng((seed + 0x85ebca6b) >>> 0) }
 11523	   157	}
 11524	   158	
 11525	   159	function draw<T>(items: readonly T[], streams: Streams, stream: 'expand' | 'tie' | 'world'): T {
 11526	   160	  const [i, next] = nextInt(streams[stream], items.length)
 11527	   161	  streams[stream] = next
 11528	   162	  return items[i] as T
 11529	   163	}
 11530	   164	
 11531	   165	export interface Selection { readonly key: ActionKey; readonly expansion: boolean }
 11532	   166	
 11533	   167	/**
 11534	   168	 * Pick one available action at `node`. Untried actions come first (one expansion per simulation), then UCB.
 11535	   169	 *
 11536	   170	 * `available` is sorted with the total `compareKeys` before anything random happens: an unsorted candidate list
 11537	   171	 * would make the uniform draw depend on the order `candidateCommands` happened to emit in THIS determinisation,
 11538	   172	 * which is exactly the kind of hidden non-determinism D-8 is about.
 11539	   173	 */
 11540	   174	export function selectKey(node: SearchNode, available: readonly ActionKey[], root: PlayerId, c: number, streams: Streams): Selection {
 11541	   175	  const keys = [...available].sort(compareKeys)
 11542	   176	  if (keys.length === 0) throw new Error('selectKey: no available actions')
 11543	   177	  const untried = keys.filter((k) => (node.edges.get(k)?.visits ?? 0) === 0)
 11544	   178	  if (untried.length) return { key: draw(untried, streams, 'expand'), expansion: true }
 11545	   179	  const actorIsRoot = node.actor === root
 11546	   180	  let best: ActionKey[] = []
 11547	   181	  let bestScore = Number.NEGATIVE_INFINITY
 11548	   182	  for (const key of keys) {
 11549	   183	    const score = ucb(edgeFor(node, key), actorIsRoot, c)
 11550	   184	    if (score > bestScore) { bestScore = score; best = [key] }
 11551	   185	    else if (score === bestScore) best.push(key)
 11552	   186	  }
 11553	   187	  return { key: best.length === 1 ? (best[0] as ActionKey) : draw(best, streams, 'tie'), expansion: false }
 11554	   188	}

 11556	   190	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 11557	   191	// Views without the clone
 11558	   192	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 11559	   193	
 11560	   194	/**
 11561	   195	 * `viewFor`'s projection minus its final `structuredClone`. The clone is ~all of a `viewFor` call (the same
 11562	   196	 * ~100 µs the review measured for `determinise`), and the search builds one view per simulated state — so
 11563	   197	 * cloning here would cost more than everything else in the search put together.
 11564	   198	 *
 11565	   199	 * Sound because nothing downstream mutates: `apply` is immutable (structural sharing), and `keys.ts` only ever
 11566	   200	 * reads. The one thing this MUST get right is which cards are visible, because that is what makes an opponent's
 11567	   201	 * hand card unnameable (`?`) instead of leaking into a key — so `test/ismcts-search.test.ts` asserts key-for-key
 11568	   202	 * agreement with `viewFor` across a whole self-play trace rather than trusting the duplication.
 11569	   203	 */
 11570	   204	export function searchView(state: GameState, me: PlayerId): PlayerView {
 11571	   205	  const field = (p: PlayerId): FieldView => {
 11572	   206	    const ps = state.players[p]
 11573	   207	    return { forwards: ps.forwards, backups: ps.backups, damageZone: ps.damageZone, breakZone: ps.breakZone, deckCount: ps.deck.length, handCount: ps.hand.length }
 11574	   208	  }
 11575	   209	  const cards: Record<CardId, CardInstance> = {}
 11576	   210	  const see = (id: CardId): void => { const inst = state.cards[id]; if (inst) cards[id] = inst }
 11577	   211	  for (const id of state.players[me].hand) see(id)
 11578	   212	  for (const p of [0, 1] as const) {
 11579	   213	    const ps = state.players[p]
 11580	   214	    for (const c of ps.forwards) see(c.id)
 11581	   215	    for (const c of ps.backups) see(c.id)
 11582	   216	    for (const id of ps.damageZone) see(id)
 11583	   217	    for (const id of ps.breakZone) see(id)
 11584	   218	  }
 11585	   219	  return {
 11586	   220	    me, turn: state.turn, turnPlayer: state.turnPlayer, phase: state.phase, attack: state.attack, priority: state.priority,
 11587	   221	    pending: state.pending, resolution: state.resolution, result: state.result, hand: state.players[me].hand,
 11588	   222	    fields: [field(0), field(1)], cards, defs: state.defs, firstPlayer: state.firstPlayer,
 11589	   223	    mulliganDecided: [state.players[0].mulliganDecided, state.players[1].mulliganDecided],
 11590	   224	  }
 11591	   225	}

 11593	   227	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 11594	   228	// Reward and rollout
 11595	   229	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 11596	   230	
 11597	   231	export interface Counters {
 11598	   232	  determinisations: number
 11599	   233	  treeApplies: number
 11600	   234	  rolloutApplies: number
 11601	   235	  evaluations: number
 11602	   236	  nodes: number
 11603	   237	  maxCommandDepth: number
 11604	   238	}
 11605	   239	
 11606	   240	const newCounters = (): Counters => ({ determinisations: 0, treeApplies: 0, rolloutApplies: 0, evaluations: 0, nodes: 0, maxCommandDepth: 0 })
 11607	   241	
 11608	   242	/**
 11609	   243	 * The root player's reward for a finished simulation, bounded to [0, 1] (D-5). Terminals are exact — 1 / 0 / ½
 11610	   244	 * — and everything else is the squashed heuristic, so the two are commensurable.
 11611	   245	 */
 11612	   246	export function leafReward(state: GameState, root: PlayerId, weights: Weights = DEFAULT_WEIGHTS, counters?: Counters | undefined): number {
 11613	   247	  if (state.result) return state.result.winner === null ? 0.5 : state.result.winner === root ? 1 : 0
 11614	   248	  if (counters) counters.evaluations++
 11615	   249	  return 0.5 + 0.5 * Math.tanh(evaluate(state, root, weights, ROLLOUT_AGGRESSION) / REWARD_SCALE)
 11616	   250	}
 11617	   251	
 11618	   252	export interface RolloutResult {
 11619	   253	  readonly state: GameState
 11620	   254	  readonly reward: number
 11621	   255	  /** Commands the rollout POLICY chose. Bounded by `cap` — that is the D-6 guarantee. */
 11622	   256	  readonly commands: number
 11623	   257	  /** Every `apply` the rollout spent, `greedyStep`'s own candidate scoring included. The real cost number. */
 11624	   258	  readonly applies: number
 11625	   259	}
 11626	   260	
 11627	   261	/**
 11628	   262	 * Greedy play for both sides past the expansion frontier (D-6), then `evaluate`.
 11629	   263	 *
 11630	   264	 * `greedyStep` answers prompts here, and ONLY here — this is past the frontier, so nothing it decides can
 11631	   265	 * consume a decision the tree was supposed to make (D-3). The cap counts chosen commands rather than applies
 11632	   266	 * or plies because an ability cascade makes one command arbitrarily expensive and one ply arbitrarily deep.
 11633	   267	 *
 11634	   268	 * The final `resolveForcedDecisions` is deliberately exempt from the cap, exactly as it is in `greedyStep`
 11635	   269	 * (greedy's W1/R4): a rollout that stops on the command after `declareAttack` would otherwise hand `evaluate` a
 11636	   270	 * board where the attack was declared, both Forwards are dull and no damage has been dealt — which prices an
 11637	   271	 * attack as pure loss and inverts the search's entire view of combat.
 11638	   272	 */
 11639	   273	export function rolloutToCap(
 11640	   274	  state: GameState, root: PlayerId, cap: number, weights: Weights = DEFAULT_WEIGHTS,
 11641	   275	  counters?: Counters | undefined, applyCap: number = DEFAULT_ROLLOUT_APPLY_CAP,
 11642	   276	): RolloutResult {
 11643	   277	  // TWO bounds, because one cannot do both jobs.
 11644	   278	  //
 11645	   279	  // `cap` bounds trajectory COMMANDS — how far into the future this rollout looks. It cannot bound the
 11646	   280	  // settlement tail below, because a state owing a block, a party split or an ability target MUST be resolved
 11647	   281	  // before `leafReward` prices it: evaluating a half-resolved position is the R4/C1/C2 defect, and stopping
 11648	   282	  // mid-cascade to respect a command budget would reintroduce it deliberately.
 11649	   283	  //
 11650	   284	  // `applyCap` bounds WORK, and it is the one that actually protects a Worker from an unbounded tail. It was
 11651	   285	  // `Infinity` — a counter, not a limit — so after the command cap the settlement tail ran without any bound
 11652	   286	  // at all, and `greedyStep` inside it applies every candidate it scores. With a real cap, `within(budget)`
 11653	   287	  // degrades that to scoring only the first candidate (rung A's W1 floor): the tail still COMPLETES, so the
 11654	   288	  // leaf is always fully resolved, it just chooses more cheaply once the budget is gone. Settlement itself
 11655	   289	  // terminates because every forced decision strictly advances, and a true cascade cycle is caught by the
 11656	   290	  // engine's own `MAX_RESOLUTION_STEPS`.
 11657	   291	  const budget = { used: 0, cap: applyCap }
 11658	   292	  let s = state
 11659	   293	  let commands = 0
 11660	   294	  while (!s.result && commands < cap) {
 11661	   295	    const p = actingPlayer(s)
 11662	   296	    if (p === null) break
 11663	   297	    const c = greedyStep(s, p, weights, ROLLOUT_AGGRESSION, budget)
 11664	   298	    if (!c) break
 11665	   299	    s = apply(s, c).state
 11666	   300	    budget.used++
 11667	   301	    commands++
 11668	   302	  }
 11669	   303	  if (!s.result) s = resolveForcedDecisions(s, weights, ROLLOUT_AGGRESSION, root, budget)
 11670	   304	  if (counters) counters.rolloutApplies += budget.used
 11671	   305	  return { state: s, reward: leafReward(s, root, weights, counters), commands, applies: budget.used }
 11672	   306	}

 11675	   309	// The search
 11676	   310	// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
 11677	   311	
 11678	   312	export interface SearchTree {
 11679	   313	  /** Exposed for tests (D-A2): the properties that matter here are structural, not win-rate-shaped. */
 11680	   314	  readonly root: SearchNode
 11681	   315	  readonly result: SearchResult
 11682	   316	}
 11683	   317	
 11684	   318	/** The declared list is a MULTISET (D-9); `determinise` samples in caller order, so sort a copy of each. */
 11685	   319	const sortedDecks = (decks: SearchInput['decks']): [string[], string[]] =>
 11686	   320	  [[...decks[0]].sort(compareKeys), [...decks[1]].sort(compareKeys)]
 11687	   321	
 11688	   322	const actorOf = (view: PlayerView): PlayerId => view.pending?.player ?? view.priority

 11690	   324	/**
 11691	   325	 * Root actions best-first (D-5): most VISITS, never best mean. The visit count is the robust statistic — an

 11694	   328	 * answer never depends on `Map` insertion order (D-8). Unvisited edges (available, never selected) are dropped.
 11695	   329	 */
 11696	   330	export function rankRootEdges(edges: readonly SearchEdge[]): SearchEdge[] {
 11697	   331	  return edges.filter((e) => e.visits > 0).sort((a, b) => b.visits - a.visits || compareKeys(a.key, b.key))
 11698	   332	}

 11700	   334	export function searchTree(input: SearchInput): SearchTree {

 11806	   440	  // Return the command the tree actually EVALUATED, not a fresh decode of its key. Keys sort their lists

 11809	   443	  // decode could hand back `[V-F1,V-F7]` where the simulations had scored `[V-F7,V-F1]` — a different

 11962	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-c3-deck-knowledge.md-40-| # | Decision | Ruling (and why) |
 11963	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-c3-deck-knowledge.md-41-|---|---|---|
 11964	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-c3-deck-knowledge.md-42-| C3-1 | **Knowledge is per player, and lives in the view's deck** | `FieldView.deckCount: number` becomes `FieldView.deck: readonly (CardId \| null)[]` — one slot per card, non-null **only** where that viewer legitimately knows what is there. The count is `deck.length`, so nothing is lost. This is the minimal representation that can express "I know my top 3 but not my fourth", which is precisely what Reeve creates. |
 11965	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-c3-deck-knowledge.md-43-| C3-2 | **`determinise` pins what is known and samples the rest** | Non-null slots keep their id and code and are removed from the unseen multiset before shuffling, exactly as field and hand cards already are (`determinise.ts:38`). Everything else is sampled as today. Without this, an AI that looked at its own top 3 would re-randomise them the instant it tried to think about them — the search would be reasoning about a deck it had just been told it did not have. |
 11966	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-c3-deck-knowledge.md:44:| C3-3 | **`viewFor` redacts pending candidates the viewer cannot see** | A `chooseTargets` whose candidates include hidden cards is filtered to those visible **to that viewer**, and carries `hidden: number` for the remainder. The opponent of a Reeve therefore sees "choosing 1 of 3 cards" and no identities. Redaction happens at the view boundary, not at the prompt, because the view boundary is the only place that knows who is asking. |
 11967	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-c3-deck-knowledge.md:45:| C3-4 | **A private choice by the OPPONENT must key on what was observed, not on what was sampled** | In ISMCTS, an opponent's private deck choice is re-sampled every determinisation. Keyed by card identity, one real decision would shatter into dozens of tree nodes that the searcher can never tell apart in play — and each would be conditioned on information the searcher does not have. Action keys for a non-root player's private choice collapse to the observable form (`take 1 of N from deck`). This is the D2 review's warning that "Reeve's private look invalidates the search's assumption that every action becomes public", answered. |
 11968	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-c3-deck-knowledge.md-46-| C3-5 | **`reveal` and `look at` are one primitive with a visibility flag** | `lookAt { count, visibility: 'public' \| 'private', filter, take }`. Public grants the knowledge to both players, private only to the controller. Building these as two effects would duplicate the ordering, filtering and bottoming logic to express a difference of one field. |
 11969	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-c3-deck-knowledge.md-47-| C3-6 | **MVP0-SIMPLIFICATION: "in any order" becomes a fixed order** | The rest go to the bottom in their revealed order; the player is not asked to arrange them. Asking would add a permutation decision (4 cards = 24 orderings) to every Miner, for cards going to the **bottom of a 40+ card deck**, which in a game this length will almost never be drawn. Marked `MVP0-SIMPLIFICATION` at the site with this reasoning, and listed in the README's deviations. |
 11970	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-c3-deck-knowledge.md-48-| C3-7 | Not in scope | **Hugh Yurg** (searches the *whole* deck, and *plays* the card onto the field rather than taking it to hand — that needs a put-into-play-without-paying effect); **Cloud's Attack-Phase clause** (needs attack entry split into preparation + continuation); EX Burst; Sphene; the "in any order" prompt. |

 11975	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.md-15-## Decisions
 11976	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.md-16-
 11977	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.md-17-| # | Decision | Ruling (and why) |
 11978	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.md-18-|---|---|---|
 11979	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.md:19:| D-1 | **SO-ISMCTS**, tree keyed on the root player's information set | Nodes are `(parent history, ActionKey, ObservationKey)`. No state transpositions initially. |
 11980	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.md:20:| D-2 | **Node identity is semantic, never by `CardId`** | This is the crux of the rung. `Command` embeds `CardId` throughout, and each determinisation assigns fresh sequential synthetic ids — so the same numeric id can mean **different cards in different worlds** (false matches) and the same semantic card can get **different ids** (false splits). `ActionKey` encodes: public zone + position for field and Break-Zone cards; **card code + occurrence** for private-hand casts and discards; normalised (sorted) sets for attackers, payments, targets and assignments. `ObservationKey` is a canonical `PlayerView` digest with every id — including in `attack`, `pending` and `resolution` — replaced by a canonical reference. Keys are decoded against the *current* determinisation; the real root `Command` is what gets returned. |
 11981	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.md-21-| D-3 | **Every `Pending` is a tree ply, whoever owns it** | Revision 1 said nodes exist only where `pending === null`, draining forced decisions first. That is backwards and dangerous: blocks, party-damage splits and ability mode/target prompts are genuine player decisions, and **at the search root, draining would have had `greedyStep` consume the very command `decide` was called to choose**. `settle()` already runs all system-only work to idle-or-prompt, so the state `apply` returns *is* the next decision boundary. Determinisation chooses hidden cards and deck order — **never a player action**. Greedy answers prompts only *past the expansion frontier*, in rollout. |
 11982	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.md-22-| D-4 | **UCB1 with availability, stated exactly** | `UCB(s,a) = mean(s,a) + C · sqrt( log A(s,a) / N(s,a) )`, where `N` is times selected and `A` is visits to `s` on which that canonical action was present in `candidateCommands`. **Availability is incremented for every compatible sibling on backpropagation**, not just the selected one; `N`/`W` only along the selected path. Revision 1 said "divide by availability", which is simply wrong — availability replaces the parent-visit count *inside the logarithm*. A win-rate gate cannot detect this being wrong, so it gets a deterministic toy test with one always-available and one rarely-available action. |
 11983	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.md-23-| D-5 | **Bounded, actor-aware rewards** | `evaluate` returns ±100,000 at terminals on an arbitrary material scale; with `C ≈ 1` one terminal rollout swamps exploration. Backpropagate a **bounded root reward**: terminal `1/0/½`, and `tanh(evaluate / scale)` at the depth cap. At root-controlled nodes maximise the mean; at **opponent-controlled nodes maximise its negation** — otherwise the search builds a cooperative opponent. `C`, the expansion rule, the final root choice (**highest visit count**) and tie-breaking are all specified, not left to the implementation. |
 11984	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.md-24-| D-6 | **Rollouts are greedy and hard-bounded** | `greedyStep` for both players past the frontier, with an explicit **cap on rollout commands**, not just a depth description — ability cascades make "depth" a poor proxy for work. Then `evaluate`. |
 11985	docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.md-25-| D-7 | **A pure, serialisable search core** | `searchIsmcts(input): { command, diagnostics }` — synchronous, no callbacks, no timing dependencies, inputs and results structured-cloneable — plus a thin stateful `IsmctsAgent` wrapper implementing `Agent`. The D2 worker protocol is **defined now**: one-time init for decks and definitions, then `{ requestId, view, seed/decisionIndex, iterations }` requests with generation-checked results. D2 then owns cancellation and React changes only. |
 11986	--

 11990	docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.codex-review.md-5-**SO-ISMCTS is a reasonable fit, but raw `Command` or move-sequence keys are unsound; this is the crux.**
 11991	docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.codex-review.md-6-
 11992	docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.codex-review.md:7:`Command` embeds `CardId` throughout (`packages/engine/src/commands.ts:4-17`). Each determinisation shuffles unseen codes and then assigns sequential synthetic IDs (`packages/engine/src/determinise.ts:31-45`). Numeric IDs may repeat between worlds while referring to different card codes, and the same semantic card/action may receive different IDs. Raw object identity never matches; structural equality produces both false matches and false splits. Move sequence alone also merges distinct observations because drawing happens automatically during turn advancement (`packages/engine/src/phases.ts:33-41`). SO-ISMCTS requires root-player information sets, not determinised state identities ([Cowling et al.](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/75048/1/CowlingPowleyWhitehouse2012.pdf)).

 12014	docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-c1-abilities.codex-code-review.md-5-**`settle()` can break a chosen target before resuming the effect that targeted it.** Ramuh may select damage then Haste and legally target the same 5000-power Forward for both (`packages/cards/src/abilities.ts:176`, `packages/cards/src/abilities.ts:180`). The second prompt is exposed while lethal damage remains (`packages/engine/src/resolve.ts:177`), but after its answer `settle()` runs rule processes before resuming (`packages/engine/src/apply.ts:36`), removes the target, and `grantKeyword` silently skips it (`packages/engine/src/resolve.ts:239`). A direct probe reproduced the stale candidate and missing Haste event. **Fix:** When an answer clears an ability pending, resume the active frame before running rule processes; keep the frame logically atomic across UI commands, then run the trailing rule-process pass after it finishes.

 12018	docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-c1-abilities.codex-code-review.md:9:**The transition snapshot implementation watches the card that moved, not cards observing the move.** `enqueueZoneTriggers` looks up abilities on `t.card` (`packages/engine/src/rules.ts:61`), whereas Lightning’s trigger belongs to a potentially different Forward watching an opponent’s card enter the Break Zone (`packages/cards/data/cards.json:272`). This also loses Lightning if both cards leave simultaneously—the exact prior-review hazard. Direct `breakCard` bypasses transitions entirely (`packages/engine/src/resolve.ts:220`), while every current transition records a null cause (`packages/engine/src/rules.ts:49`). **Fix:** Snapshot all pre-transition trigger sources, match their abilities against the complete transition batch, and route direct breaks/returns and damage-caused moves through one source-aware transition pipeline.
 12019	docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-c1-abilities.codex-code-review.md-10-
 12020	docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-c1-abilities.codex-code-review.md-11-**The budget-starved Ramuh mode policy can choose a provably redundant pair.** Modes are valued independently and summed (`packages/ai/src/candidates.ts:205`), then the highest individual modes become the first answer (`packages/ai/src/candidates.ts:237`). Against an active 5000-power Prishe with a fresh friendly Forward, it ranks damage+dull first even though both target Prishe; damage+Haste kills the same card and unlocks an attacker. An exhausted budget scores only that first answer (`packages/ai/src/greedy.ts:87`). The separate chip-vs-kill defect is fixed at `packages/ai/src/candidates.ts:111`. **Fix:** Enumerate the at-most-seven Ramuh mode subsets and rank each jointly, applying its nested target policy in printed order so interactions and redundancy are visible.

 12022	docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-c1-abilities.codex-code-review.md-13-**A continuation by itself is treated as settled and becomes permanently orphaned.** `settle()` exits and resets based only on `active` and `queue` (`packages/engine/src/apply.ts:39`, `packages/engine/src/apply.ts:45`), although `drainResolution` is the only code that consumes the continuation (`packages/engine/src/resolve.ts:324`). AI diagnostics likewise count only frames (`packages/ai/src/greedy.ts:130`). A probe left `enterAttackDeclaration` in `main1` indefinitely with invariants still green. **Fix:** Introduce a shared `hasResolutionWork()` including `continuation`; use it in settlement, invariants, and AI diagnostics.  12029	docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.codex-code-review.md:5:**`decodeAction` can return an observably different command from the one the tree evaluated.** List-valued commands are sorted into keys (`packages/ai/src/ismcts/keys.ts:214`, `:224`, `:226`, `:228`), simulations apply the original candidate (`packages/ai/src/ismcts/search.ts:372`, `:377`), but the final result prefers a freshly decoded command (`packages/ai/src/ismcts/search.ts:417`). Decoding consumes refs in sorted-key order (`packages/ai/src/ismcts/keys.ts:357`, `:376`), while the engine preserves command order in the Break Zone and resolution frame (`packages/engine/src/cp.ts:105`, `packages/engine/src/phases.ts:79`, `packages/engine/src/resolve.ts:485`). `observationKey` then treats Break-Zone order as significant (`packages/ai/src/ismcts/keys.ts:407`). A direct probe showed `[V-F7,V-F1]` being evaluated, decoded as `[V-F1,V-F7]`, and producing different Break-Zone observations. The round-trip test checks only re-keying and legality, not transition equivalence (`packages/ai/test/ismcts-keys.test.ts:264`). **Fix:** Return `rootCommands.get(best.key)` as the authoritative live command, or canonicalize/decode commands before every tree `apply`. Add tests comparing post-apply `ObservationKey`s for original versus decoded casts, discards, targets, and assignments.
 12030	docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.codex-code-review.md-6-
 12031	docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-27-rung-d1-ismcts.codex-code-review.md-7-**The rollout command cap is not a hard bound.** `rolloutToCap` gives Greedy an infinite internal budget and, after reaching the cap, invokes an exempt `resolveForcedDecisions` tail (`packages/ai/src/ismcts/search.ts:266`, `:278`). That helper selects and applies actual player commands (`packages/ai/src/greedy.ts:71`, `:77`, `:79`). The test explicitly demonstrates `cap: 0` performing additional applies while still reporting zero commands (`packages/ai/test/ismcts-search.test.ts:367`, `:371`, `:375`). This violates D-6 and creates exactly the unbounded work tail that will hurt Worker latency/cancellation. **Fix:** Count every trajectory command, including forced prompts, against the cap; use a bounded pending-aware leaf evaluation or a separately bounded settlement allowance. Add a hard apply/work cap as the Worker-facing safety bound.

 13338	    84	export function runRuleProcesses(state: GameState): [GameState, Event[]] {

 13345	    91	    if (!transitions.length) break

 13349	    95	    // controller whose field it was removed from. Owner and controller coincide for the whole MVP0 pool (nothing
 13350	    96	    // changes control yet), so this is unobservable today — but the transitions already carry both, and taking
 13351	    97	    // the controller here was the bug that made "capture owner properly" only half-done.
